common_name: Mrs. Hegarty Crimson Flag Lily (Soft Pink Hesperantha)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions 1-2 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near pond margins, stream banks, or moist border edges; Mrs. Hegarty is one of the oldest and most widely grown named selections of crimson flag lily and thrives wherever soil stays reliably moist through summer.

directions: Mrs. Hegarty is one of the oldest and most widely grown named selections of crimson flag lily (formerly Schizostylis coccinea), valued for its clear, soft shell-pink, star-shaped flowers carried on slender stems from late summer into fall, a gentler counterpart to the brighter scarlet of the species and the larger, deeper red 'Major'. Its grassy, strap-like evergreen leaves persist through mild winters, and clumps bulk up steadily from spreading rhizomes, benefiting from division every three years or so to maintain vigor and control spread. Like other crimson flag lily selections it demands consistent summer moisture and will sulk in dry soil, but rewards a moist site with dependable, welcome color late in the season when little else in the border is blooming.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plants Database

common_name: Major Crimson Flag Lily (Large Red Hesperantha)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions 1-2 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near pond margins, stream banks, or moist border edges; Major is a classic, long-grown crimson flag lily selection valued for the size and saturation of its red flowers.

directions: Major is a classic, long-grown selection of crimson flag lily (formerly Schizostylis coccinea) prized for its large, brilliant deep-red, star-shaped flowers, bigger and more saturated in color than the species and the softer pink of 'Mrs. Hegarty', carried on slender stems from late summer into fall. Its strap-like, grassy leaves stay evergreen in mild climates, and established clumps spread steadily by rhizome, needing division every few years to stay vigorous and within bounds. Like other crimson flag lily selections, Major performs best with consistent summer moisture and struggles in soil that dries out, making it a natural fit for pond edges, stream banks, and the damp edge of a rain garden where its late-season color is especially valuable.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plants Database

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep and 8-10 inches apart in sharply well-drained, alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in a warm, sheltered, full-sun position in fall; 'Adiyaman' is a named selection of Persian fritillary collected from the Adiyaman region of southeastern Turkey.

directions: 'Adiyaman' is a named selection of Persian fritillary collected from the Adiyaman region of southeastern Turkey, prized among fritillary growers for an especially dark, near-black plum-purple flower color and for flowering more freely and reliably than typical seed-grown Persian fritillary. It carries the same stout, upright stems clothed in whorls of glaucous blue-grey leaves and topped by a long raceme of 20-30 or more pendant, bell-shaped flowers as the species, but its deeper, richer color and improved flowering habit have made it one of the more sought-after forms in specialty bulb catalogs. Like the species, it demands sharp drainage and a hot, dry summer rest to thrive, rotting quickly in heavy or waterlogged soil, and performs best in a raised bed or gritty border where its architectural height and unmatched flower color can be appreciated up close.
